ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all UBOs, directors, officers and authorized signatories against: (i) the UN Security Council Consolidated List; (ii) the US OFAC SDN List and all applicable OFAC sanctions programs; (iii) the Canadian Consolidated Sanctions List published under the Special Economic Measures Act, the United Nations Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act; and (iv) the FATF public statements and regional PEP databases. Enhanced due diligence is mandatory for domestic and foreign politically exposed persons (PEPs), their family members and close associates, requiring documented source of wealth and source of funds. Continuous re-screening and transaction monitoring are required under the PCMLTFA and supporting regulations.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry — CorpeService online portal (via alberta.ca)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The proposed corporate name must use Latin script and include a distinctive element and the mandatory legal element 'ULC' or 'Unlimited Liability Corporation' in English or French. Names in non-Roman scripts must be transliterated to the Roman alphabet; Chinese, Cyrillic or Arabic script names are not registrable. The name must not be identical or confusing with any existing corporate, trade, or business name registered in Alberta.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon rejection, the applicant may file a Corporate Name Review Request with the Alberta Corporate Registry within 15 business days of the refusal, submitting legal arguments and a new NUANS report if the prior report has expired. The Registrar will issue a written decision within 15 business days. If the refusal is upheld, the applicant may apply for judicial review before the Court of King's Bench of Alberta, and where the name is in use by an existing corporation, may apply for court-ordered rectification or injunction under the Alberta Business Corporations Act.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permitted only where the provider operates a physical, staffed street address in Alberta at which legal process may be served during normal business hours; pure mail-forwarding or non-staffed virtual offices do not satisfy the ABCA registered office requirements. For ISIC 6311 (digital app business), a compliant virtual office is generally acceptable for the registered office, provided the corporate records and registers are available for inspection at that address.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low quantifiable risk for the video-chat digital app industry because the business has no public-facing premises and all records are maintained by a statutory agent; the annual probability of an unannounced physical inspection by Alberta Corporate Registry or FINTRAC is assessed at 5%, subject to increased risk if the registered office is non-responsive or financial reports are not filed timely.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), R.S.A. 2000, c. B-9, as amended; Part 1 (incorporation), ss. 8, 9, 14 and 24; capital provisions applicable to unlimited liability corporations; ss. 101, 113, 118 and 124 respecting directors, officers and corporate records.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry (Service Alberta, Government of Alberta)
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation filed under the Alberta Business Corporations Act together with the required NUANS name search report and registered office information, incorporating the unlimited liability corporation (ULC) designation.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No minimum paid-up capital and no statutory escrow account are required under Alberta law. Shares may be issued with or without par value and for such consideration as the directors determine, provided that shares are not issued until fully paid and the consideration received is adequate.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED: the completion of the Corporation’s incorporation by the Certificate of Incorporation is ratified and approved. RESOLVED: the shares set out in the subscription ledger are subscribed for and issued for the agreed consideration, each subscriber having executed the required unlimited liability acknowledgment. RESOLVED: the registered office in Alberta is adopted at the address in the articles, and the registered office information is authorized for filing with the Registrar. RESOLVED: the persons named in the organization minutes are appointed Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and Corporate Secretary until successors are elected; management is authorized to execute implementing documents.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Name Search Review and NUANS Reservation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry – NUANS Name Search
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS preliminary name search through a licensed Alberta Registry Agent or the authorized online corporate search platform. Review the search report for confusing names and obtain a 90-day name reservation if the desired name is available. For a no-name incorporation, proceed with a numbered company.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused as confusing, choose an alternate name from the search report or use a corporate number name; file a new NUANS reservation if an alternate name is desired.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting Articles of Incorporation with ULC Designation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry (Service Alberta) / licensed legal counsel
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the Alberta Articles of Incorporation with the corporate name, physical registered office address in Alberta, share structure, first directors, and the express unlimited liability designation required for a ULC. Confirm that no par value or minimum paid-up capital is imposed and that the articles comply with ABCA content requirements.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar identifies omitted statutory particulars, revise and re-file the articles; if the ULC designation is missing, amend the articles before submission to avoid a defective share liability feature.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing Articles and Obtaining Certificate of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the executed Articles of Incorporation electronically or in person to the Alberta Corporate Registry, pay the statutory incorporation fee, and receive the Certificate of Incorporation. The certificate is conclusive proof of incorporation and identifies the date on which the Corporation came into existence.
required_dossiers: Registered office information form if not included in articles
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried, respond to the Registrar’s deficiency notice within the specified period by filing a corrected application; the filing fee is applied to the processing attempt and is not refunded.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Organizational Meeting of First Directors and Adoption of Bylaws
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Hold the organizational meeting of the first directors. The directors shall adopt the corporate by-laws, fix the fiscal year-end, elect officers, approve the minute book and share certificates, and authorize the opening of the corporate bank account. All organizational resolutions must be recorded in the minute book.
required_dossiers: Consent to Act as Director forms
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a first director cannot serve, the remaining directors may appoint a substitute director in accordance with ABCA; update the notice of directors and make a conforming organizational resolution.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registered Office and Statutory Records Establishment
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Maintain a registered office at a physical address in Alberta; post office boxes are not acceptable. If the articles did not already state the registered office, file the Notice of Registered Office. Keep the corporate records, register of directors, shareholder register, and governing documents at the registered office or in another suitable records place permitted by the ABCA.
required_dossiers: Notice of Registered Office or confirmation in articles
Proof of physical address or registered agent consent
Corporate minute book and statutory registers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the address is non-compliant, file a Notice of Change of Registered Office with a compliant physical address and provide landlord or registered agent consent to the Registry agent.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Share Subscription and Unlimited Liability Acknowledgment
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors and founding subscribers
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Issue the initially subscribed shares to the founding shareholders in accordance with the first board resolution. Each subscriber must sign an acknowledgment stating that the Corporation carries on with unlimited liability for its shareholders and that the shares are subject to ABCA rules. Enter the allotments in the shareholder register and issue share certificates.
required_dossiers: Share certificates and register of shareholders
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a subscriber does not pay the agreed consideration, withhold issuance; if a signed unlimited liability acknowledgment is missing, collect it before delivering the share certificate or rescind the allotment and reissue to a compliant subscriber.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: CRA Tax Accounts, WCB Registration, and Municipal Business Licence
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency; Alberta Workers’ Compensation Board; municipal business licensing office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Apply for the federal Business Number and required corporate income tax and GST/HST accounts with the CRA. Register the employer account with the Alberta Workers’ Compensation Board if employees will be engaged. File any municipal business licence application if a physical business address or signage is used, and obtain building and fire occupancy approvals if required.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA account setup is delayed, contact the CRA business window with the incorporation number; if the municipal licence is queried, supply the certificate, insurance certificate, and landlord confirmation of occupancy and rectify any structural or fire safety deficiencies.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: None applicable — no Alberta provincially mandated industrial licensing board applies to ISIC 6311 software/video-match operations.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No sectoral statutory operating license is required for the Real-Time Video Matching and Cross-Border Social Telephony application; only a general municipal Business Licence may apply if a physical office is operated.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt / Registration only — the activity is low-impact commercial office use and does not trigger a Full Environmental Impact Assessment under the Environmental Protection and Enhancement Act and the Activities Designation Regulation.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: No industrial process wastewater, VOCs, or combustion emissions are expected. Discharges must comply with municipal sanitary sewer-use bylaws and Alberta’s ambient air quality objectives. Electronic waste is subject to the Alberta Recycling Regulation, requiring diversion to an authorized recycler.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire and building safety clearance under the Safety Codes Act through the local authority having jurisdiction; structural occupancy load certification before office use; occupational health and safety compliance inspection under the OHSA; and registration of the employer account with the Alberta Workers’ Compensation Board.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada — federal tax authority; Business Registration Online (BRO) and My Business Account portal. GST/HST is administered exclusively by CRA; Alberta corporate income tax is collected by CRA under a single-administration agreement with the Alberta Ministry of Finance and Service Alberta Corporate Registry.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: (1) Incorporate the ULC in Alberta through Service Alberta Corporate Registry to obtain the provincial incorporation/registry number; (2) Register with CRA for a nine-digit Business Number (BN) via Business Registration Online or Form RC1, activating T2 (corporate income tax), RT (GST/HST) and RP (payroll) program accounts; (3) For a foreign-owned ULC, provide certified constitutional documents, a Canadian business address, and a duly appointed representative for service of process; (4) Register for GST/HST under the non-resident digital economy rules where taxable digital supplies to Canadian consumers exceed the CAD 30,000 threshold (mandatory as of 1 July 2021); (5) File annual T2 returns with federal and Alberta (provincial) allocation, remitting final balances and installments in CAD.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No domestic check-the-box: an Alberta ULC is automatically a taxable Canadian corporation (entity-level Part I tax; federal 15% non-CCPC general rate plus Alberta 8% equals 23% combined; Part XIII dividend withholding at 25% statutory, treaty-reduced). Pass-through eligibility is a foreign-shareholder concept: a U.S. shareholder can file Form 8832 check-the-box to treat the ULC as a disregarded entity for U.S. tax (hybrid entity), but Canada ignores that election. Available elections include: ETA s. 156 (GST/HST grouping of closely related corporations), ETA s. 211.5 (selected listed financial institution election for financial-service revenue), and ITA s. 216 (non-resident election for Canadian rental income). Canada-U.S. Treaty Article XXIX A restricts ULC treaty benefits where the ULC is fiscally transparent in the U.S.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (federal Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax); Alberta applies only the 5% federal GST component — Alberta has no provincial sales tax or provincial HST component
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 — small-supplier threshold over the current and four preceding calendar quarters for worldwide taxable supplies made in Canada (zero-rated export supplies count toward the threshold; a ULC exporting digital video-matching services above CAD 30,000 must register for GST/HST); non-resident digital-platform suppliers have the same CAD 30,000 mandatory registration trigger for Canadian consumer taxable supplies, effective 1 July 2021
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping, or mandatory government-authorised continuous transaction control (CTC) e-invoicing API in Canada. CRA permits electronic invoices where the recipient consents; the Pan-Canadian e-Invoice standard (PEPPOL BIS 3.0) is voluntary, with a CRA phased adoption roadmap but no current statutory mandate. GST/HST returns must be filed electronically (GST34 via NETFILE or My Business Account) and payments remitted in CAD to CRA.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Goods: zero-rated under Schedule VI Part V of the Excise Tax Act where exported by the supplier, delivered to a common carrier for export, or sold to a non-resident for export (normally leaving Canada within 60 days) with documentary evidence per GST/HST Memorandum 17.5.2. Services: zero-rated under Schedule VI Part V s. 7 where supplied to a non-resident and not performed in relation to Canadian real property or unexported goods — real-time video-matching app access, platform subscriptions, and related digital telephony services supplied from Canada to non-residents qualify for 0% GST/HST. The supplier must evidence the customer's non-resident status, offshore delivery/consumption of the digital service, and payment terms.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: CBSA Customs Export Declaration (Canadian Export Reporting System / CAED) or B13A for controlled or regulated goods
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill evidencing physical export and date of departure
Commercial invoice and zero-rating certificate (CRA export evidence per GST/HST Memorandum 17.5.2)
Inward Remittance Certificate / SWIFT wire record evidencing collection of export proceeds in freely convertible currency
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA denies zero-rating and claws back output GST plus previously refunded input tax credits where the documentation bundle is incomplete. Reassessments within four years (or unlimited for misrepresentation) plus interest; ETA s. 280 penalty of the greater of CAD 250 and 25% of net tax for false statements or omissions; gross-negligence penalties; criminal exposure under ETA s. 331. CBSA Administrative Monetary Penalties up to CAD 25,000 per export-reporting violation. CRA reviews export proceeds received beyond the 180-day benchmark as an indicator of undisclosed foreign receivables or non-export transactions, which can trigger transfer-pricing, deemed-dividend, and foreign-affiliate recharacterization adjustments.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada; Canada has no separate foreign exchange administration imposing general capital controls or mandatory currency surrender requirements.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is generally fully convertible for current-account and capital-account transactions. A Canadian Alberta unlimited liability corporation may generally receive foreign capital, pay foreign suppliers, remit dividends, repay shareholder loans, and purchase foreign currency, subject to corporate law, solvency requirements, tax withholding, sanctions, anti-money-laundering controls, beneficial-ownership verification, transfer-pricing rules, and bank-specific transaction monitoring. Dividends must be lawfully declared and paid from available corporate resources under applicable Alberta corporate law. Dividends, interest, royalties, and certain other payments to non-residents may require Canadian withholding tax, subject to applicable treaty relief and prescribed documentation. Cross-border related-party financing must be supported by arm's-length terms, transfer-pricing records, and appropriate thin-capitalization analysis. Foreign ownership is generally permitted, but federally regulated payment activities, sanctions exposure, national-security considerations, and regulated-sector rules may create additional requirements.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no general statutory deadline for repatriating export proceeds and no mandatory conversion ratio for export receipts. Export proceeds may generally remain in Canadian-dollar or foreign-currency accounts, subject to contractual terms, accounting records, tax reporting, sanctions compliance, and ordinary bank monitoring. Payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions or persons may be prohibited or require authorization under Canadian sanctions legislation. Customs, GST/HST, income-tax, transfer-pricing, and export-control obligations remain separate from foreign-exchange convertibility.

Operational Account; foreign-currency account and commercial treasury services; no general statutory capital escrow requirement
Operational Account; foreign-currency account, wire, trade-finance, and hedging services
Operational Account; foreign-currency account and corporate treasury services
Operational Account; foreign-currency account, payments, and treasury services
Operational Account; Alberta-focused commercial banking and foreign-exchange services, subject to product and eligibility review

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium for payment collection and payouts; low as a substitute for a Canadian corporate operating bank account. An offshore electronic-money institution does not automatically obtain the right to provide payment services in Canada. Activities within the federal Retail Payment Activities Act framework may require registration with the Bank of Canada, operational-risk and safeguarding compliance, incident reporting, and regulatory disclosures. The institution must also comply with applicable anti-money-laundering, sanctions, consumer-protection, data, and foreign-jurisdiction requirements. Canadian banks and payment processors may restrict third-party collection, money transmission, marketplace settlement, stored value, or commingling of customer funds. The entity should use a Canadian bank account for corporate capital, payroll, taxes, refunds, chargeback reserves, and settlement reconciliation, and should obtain written confirmation that Apple IAP, Paymentwall, and any other processor permit the proposed merchant-of-record and beneficiary structure.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No general Canadian statutory rule requires all directors to appear physically for corporate bank-account opening. Remote onboarding may be available, but the bank may require a video interview, notarized or certified identification, a Canadian signing officer, an in-person meeting, confirmation of the Alberta registered office, or branch attendance based on risk. Non-resident directors, an Alberta ULC, a complex ownership chain, virtual offices, high-risk countries, nominee arrangements, unexplained payment flows, or a digital-social-platform business may trigger enhanced due diligence and delay or refusal.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unclear beneficial ownership, layered foreign ownership, nominee shareholders, or inability to identify controlling persons
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified articles and certificate of incorporation, Alberta corporate registry profile, current shareholder register, ownership chart to natural persons, director and officer register, beneficial-owner declarations, government identification, proof of address, and board resolutions confirming account authority.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unlimited-liability corporation structure perceived as unusual, tax-driven, or inconsistent with the stated commercial purpose
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Alberta incorporation documents, legal memorandum describing the ULC and unlimited-liability consequences, constitutional documents, group structure chart, tax-residency analysis, commercial rationale, shareholder and director resolutions, and written confirmation of the entity's intended banking and contracting functions.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Random video-matching or social-telephony activity presenting elevated fraud, abuse, trafficking, impersonation, child-safety, or platform-integrity concerns
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Detailed product memorandum, terms of service, privacy policy, age-assurance controls, moderation and trust-and-safety policy, prohibited-content rules, reporting and escalation procedures, law-enforcement response policy, geoblocking controls, sanctions screening, user-risk controls, data-governance framework, and independent compliance contact.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unexplained payment flows involving Apple IAP, Paymentwall, offshore processors, customer refunds, chargebacks, or third-party settlement
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Processor agreements, merchant-of-record analysis, settlement-flow diagram, expected monthly volumes, countries of origin and destination, average transaction size, refund and chargeback assumptions, reserve arrangements, reconciliation procedures, sample invoices, financial projections, and confirmation that settlement beneficiaries match the corporation.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Foreign shareholder funding, shareholder loans, or large inbound wires without a clear legal and tax characterization
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed subscription agreement or loan agreement, board approvals, source-of-funds and source-of-wealth evidence, originating-bank statements, investor corporate records, beneficial-owner information, capitalization table, repayment terms, transfer-pricing support, and tax withholding analysis.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Virtual office, non-resident management, no Canadian employees, or weak evidence of Alberta business operations
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Registered-office evidence, lease or service agreement, Alberta corporate records, management biographies, operating plan, contracts, service-provider agreements, payroll or contractor records where applicable, Canadian tax registrations, and explanation of the Alberta entity's actual functions.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions, high-risk jurisdiction, politically exposed person, adverse media, or unusual cross-border transaction corridor
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Full counterparty list, sanctions-screening methodology, beneficial-owner verification, PEP and adverse-media results, transaction-purpose documentation, country-risk assessment, escalation approvals, and evidence that prohibited parties and jurisdictions are excluded.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Incomplete Canadian tax, corporate, or regulatory registrations
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Business number, GST/HST registration where required, payroll account where applicable, corporate income-tax filing status, Alberta registry filings, annual returns, foreign-ownership and statistical reporting analysis, and compliance calendar.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Route equity through a Canadian commercial bank operating account by SWIFT or correspondent-bank wire in the corporation's legal name. The payment narrative should accurately identify the transaction as paid-up capital, share subscription proceeds, or shareholder loan principal, as applicable; Canada does not use a universal statutory FX purpose-code system for ordinary corporate wires. The bank may request the subscription or loan agreement, board resolutions, capitalization table, beneficial-owner information, source-of-funds evidence, originating-bank details, and expected use of funds. The corporation should preserve wire confirmations, maintain a capital and intercompany-loan ledger, reconcile the receipt to the corporate books, and apply Canadian withholding, transfer-pricing, thin-capitalization, sanctions, and tax-reporting rules where relevant. Do not route capital through personal accounts, unrelated payment processors, or omnibus wallets. Large or unusual cash transactions and suspicious transactions may trigger reporting by the financial institution to FINTRAC.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Use Canadian bank wires through correspondent networks for ordinary supplier and service payments, with accurate beneficiary, invoice, contract, goods-or-services description, country, and tax information. SWIFT MT103 remains a commonly understood wire-payment reference, but banks increasingly process and exchange payment data under ISO 20022 formats. For higher-value or documentary trade, use a commercial letter of credit issued or advised through an eligible bank under the agreed rules, ordinarily UCP 600, with documentary requirements matching the underlying transaction. Use documentary collections, open-account wires, or supply-chain-finance arrangements only after counterparty, sanctions, fraud, and delivery risks are assessed. Maintain invoices, contracts, proof of performance or delivery, customs records where applicable, payment approvals, and reconciliation evidence. Payments to related parties require arm's-length support and transfer-pricing records; payments of interest, royalties, or other specified amounts to non-residents may require withholding and reporting.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards with an authorized Canadian bank or other properly regulated dealer, supported by a documented underlying exposure, treasury policy, counterparty limits, confirmations, valuation, and settlement controls.

Non-deliverable forwards for currencies or markets where physical delivery is impractical, subject to dealer availability, applicable Canadian derivatives rules, eligible-counterparty or commercial-hedging requirements, documented exposure, and sanctions and jurisdictional restrictions.

Currency swaps and cross-currency interest-rate swaps for recurring or long-dated currency and funding exposures, subject to ISDA documentation, collateral and margin terms where applicable, valuation controls, accounting treatment, counterparty credit limits, and applicable derivatives reporting or business-conduct requirements.

Foreign-currency options, collars, and participating forwards where commercially appropriate, with clear disclosure of premium, maximum exposure, break costs, collateral, and early-termination consequences.

Natural hedges through matching currency receipts and expenses, foreign-currency cash balances, and staggered settlement, subject to liquidity, concentration, accounting, and operational-risk controls.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the incorporation/amalgamation anniversary; anniversary-based, not calendar-year-based
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: CAD 50 late-filing fee; loss of good standing certificate; continued non-filing across two anniversaries may trigger administrative strike-off and dissolution

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within 6 months after the taxation year-end; balance-due date is 2 or 3 months after year-end depending on CCPC status
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of 5% of unpaid balance plus 1% per month for up to 12 months; repeated failure attracts 10% penalty; daily compound interest and criminal prosecution in egregious cases

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Mandatory for reporting issuers; otherwise not required by revenue or asset thresholds. A non-reporting Alberta ULC is exempt from appointing an auditor unless shareholders holding at least 5% of voting shares requisition one
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS or Canadian ASPE; a private Alberta ULC generally applies ASPE unless it has opted for IFRS or is a reporting issuer

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta does not impose a separate annual beneficial-ownership declaration. The ULC must maintain its Register of Individuals with Significant Control and record share transfers promptly; an internal register audit should reconcile the ISC register to the share register before filing the annual return
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Individuals with Significant Control

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 0 by default; USD 4,000 – USD 10,000 if the audit exemption is successfully removed or a shareholder-requested audit is engaged

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined general federal and Alberta corporate income tax rate (15% federal Part I on grossed-up taxable income plus 8% Alberta general corporate rate). For Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) claiming the small business deduction, the combined rate on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income is 11% (9% federal small business rate plus 2% Alberta small business rate).
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No statutory tax holiday or free-zone exemption exists in Canada or Alberta. Preferential reductions are available through the federal small business deduction, the Alberta small business tax rate, scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) investment tax credits, accelerated capital cost allowance rates, and the federal general rate reduction on manufacturing and processing income. An Alberta ULC is taxed for Canadian income tax purposes as a corporation and is not eligible for flow-through treatment domestically.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return plus mandatory GIFI (General Index of Financial Information) schedules; filed electronically via CRA's EFILE, Netfile for corporations is not available, or through CRA My Business Account. The T2 is the federal Part I income tax return.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual, based on the adopted federal fiscal period; a short first taxation year is permitted. The return can cover a maximum 53-week period where the corporation changes its taxation year.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The federal T2 return must be filed on or before the later of six months after the end of the taxation year and, for a corporation with a non-calendar registered future without specific exception, the six-month anniversary of the fiscal year-end. Payment of balance due is required within two months after fiscal year-end for non-CCPCs and three months for CCPCs eligible for the small business deduction.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net business income or loss per financial statements reconciled to tax basis.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations report only Canadian-source income attributable to a permanent establishment in Canada; foreign-source income is excluded from Part I tax unless treaty provisions require inclusion.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal taxable income after application of carryover losses and permanent establishment allocation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use Schedule B of the T2 to calculate the federal allocation factor for a non-resident with permanent establishments in multiple provinces.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Base federal Part I tax computed at 15% general rate or at the 9% small business rate on eligible active income below CAD 500,000.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident-controlled corporations are not eligible for the small business deduction unless they are residents of Canada and qualify as CCPCs; treaty-relief claims are made on the T2 with Form T1246 or Schedules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Final Part I tax payable after investment tax credits, foreign tax credits, and political contribution credits.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation must file Part I tax on Canadian-source business income even if the ordinary Part XIII withholding was already applied to gross proceeds.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty of 5% of the unpaid tax, increased by 1% for each complete month late up to 12 months; a repeat failure penalty of 10% may apply. Gross negligence penalties under section 163 of the Income Tax Act can be 50% of the understated tax. Prescribed interest is charged on late-filed amounts and compounded daily.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: AT1 Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (also referred to as Alberta Corporate Tax Return); filed separately with the Government of Alberta, Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, through the provincial electronic filing system for corporate taxpayers.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual, aligned with the federal taxation year; the tax returns are reconciled to the T2 filing.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The AT1 must be filed within six months after the end of the federal taxation year. Alberta corporate income tax instalments and final balance payments generally follow the federal payment schedule: two months after year-end, or three months for CCPCs entitled to the small business deduction.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provincial taxable income after application of interprovincial allocation and provincial loss pooling.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the non-resident corporation has no permanent establishment in Alberta, this amount is nil and no AT1 is required unless Alberta-source employment or property income triggers allocation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta general corporate income tax at 8% on the taxable income in Box 100.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Alberta basic tax is only charged on income with a permanent establishment in Alberta; a non-resident without an Alberta PE will have zero in this box.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reductions for CCPCs under the Alberta Small Business Deduction on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income earned in Alberta.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident-controlled corporation is not a CCPC and cannot claim the 2% reduction unless a special designation exists under the Canada-Alberta Tax Coordination Agreement.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta corporate income tax payable after all provincial tax credits and rebates.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Any Alberta tax due must be remitted to the Government of Alberta; the federal T2 return includes a reconciliation of the amount paid to Alberta, and a non-resident payor must withhold separately on dividends paid to foreign shareholders.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Alberta imposes a late filing penalty of 5% of unpaid provincial tax plus 1% per complete month up to 12 months, with interest on arrears at prescribed rates; false or incomplete AT1 filings may trigger a civil penalty of up to 25% of the provincial tax understated.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% under subsection 212(2) of the Income Tax Act, payable by the Canadian corporation on any dividend paid to a non-resident shareholder. An Alberta ULC, despite its unlimited liability structure, remains a resident corporation for Canadian tax purposes, so its distributions are dividends subject to Part XIII withholding.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke a reduced treaty withholding rate, the non-resident shareholder must complete and deliver Form NR301 (Statement of Withholding Exemption for Non-Resident Taxpayers) to the Canadian paying corporation before the dividend is paid. The form must be accompanied by evidence of residence, generally an official Tax Residency Certificate (TRC) issued by the foreign revenue authority. Under the Canada-United States Tax Convention, a US shareholder that is the beneficial owner of the dividend is entitled to a 15% rate on portfolio dividends and a 5% rate on qualifying dividends for a US corporation that owns at least 10% of the voting shares of the Canadian ULC. If ULC shareholders exercise the unlimited liability flow-through election for US federal tax purposes, Canadian Part XIII withholding remains applicable, but the US shareholder may be entitled to FTC treatment for the withheld amount.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII withholding tax is 25% on royalties paid to non-residents for the use of industrial property, patents, trademarks, software copyright, and similar intangibles. Under the Canada-United States Treaty, royalties generally are reduced to a 10% source-state rate, and certain software or cultural royalties may be taxable at 0% where they are classified as business profits. Interest paid by a Canadian ULC to an arm's-length non-resident is generally exempt from Canadian withholding tax under the arm's-length interest exemption in subparagraph 212(1)(b)(vii) of the Income Tax Act; non-arm's-length interest is subject to 25%, with a 0% or reduced rate under most modern treaties where the beneficial owner is a US resident and the interest is not contingent on profits.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Canada has no statutory monetary threshold for preparing Local File or Master File documents in advance, but CRA's transfer pricing administration (Transfer Pricing Memorandum TPM-08) expressly expects contemporaneous, complete and accurate documentation to be prepared where the aggregate controlled transactions with a particular non-resident exceed CAD 1,000,000 in a taxation year. The filing of Form T106 (Information Return for Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents) is mandatory whenever the aggregate amount of per year transactions with a non-resident exceeds CAD 1,000,000. For a digital video-matching app operating through an Alberta ULC, all intercompany fees for video content licenses, technology support, user acquisition, and payment processing services must be benchmarked at arm's length and supported with OECD-aligned documentation. CAD 1,000,000 is the operative threshold triggering T106 disclosure and CRA's enhanced documentation expectation.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not administer a stand-alone Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) regime like offshore financial centres; however, the general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) under section 245 of the Income Tax Act defeats transactions that are considered artificial, lack any business purpose, or are designed to obtain treaty benefits without commensurate economic activity. For an Alberta ULC used in a video-chat monetization structure, CRA will scrutinize the entity's payroll, office premises, decision-making, and risk absorption. The Canada-US Treaty includes a Limitation on Benefits article that requires substantive business presence. The unlimited liability feature of the ULC is not itself economic substance; the ULC must be actively managed, pay arm's-length consideration for any Canadian user data and intellectual property inflows, and maintain full corporate governance records.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately omitting Canadian-source revenue from the T2/AT1 returns, shifting app subscription and in-app advertising revenue to a non-resident related entity without arm's-length value, or falsely treating video-chat fees as non-taxable foreign source income.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under section 239 of the Income Tax Act, tax evasion is punishable by a fine of up to CAD 200,000 and imprisonment up to 5 years on indictment, plus civil reassessment and a gross negligence penalty under subsection 163(2) equal to 50% of the understated tax. The CRA may also apply the collection of unpaid taxes against the ULC's assets and directors.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior officers who knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence assisted in the evasion are jointly and severally liable for corporate tax debts under subsection 227.1(1) of the Income Tax Act. In an Alberta ULC, shareholders' unlimited liability for corporate obligations enables the CRA to pursue personal assets for tax liabilities where improper distributions or fraudulent conveyances have occurred. Travel bans can be issued upon indictment, and imprisonment applies to natural persons convicted of evasion.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to file Form T106 for controlled transactions above CAD 1,000,000, absence of contemporaneous TP documentation, or use of a non-arm's-length royalty paid to a low-tax foreign affiliate for user-list and algorithm intangibles without a comparability analysis or profit allocation that satisfies the arm's-length standard.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under subsection 247(3) of the Income Tax Act, a transfer pricing penalty of 10% of the net transfer pricing adjustment may be imposed when the adjustment exceeds CAD 1,000,000. The CRA will also reassess the ULC's taxable income upwards, disallow excessive deductions, apply interest on the reassessed balance, and impose secondary documentation penalties up to CAD 24,000 per failure to provide a complete and accurate response to a demand for TP documentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are not automatically liable for TP penalties under section 247, but if the TP adjustment gives rise to unpaid source withholding tax or Part XIII tax, directors can be held personally liable under the withholding-tax director liability regime. For an Alberta ULC, shareholders and directors are liable to creditors for the full debts and liabilities of the corporation; CRA can exercise civil tracing remedies against personal assets where the transfer pricing transactions were structured to strip the ULC of funds.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating an Alberta ULC as a shell condui with no employees, no office, no Canadian management, and no commercial activity, solely to claim reduced Canada-US treaty withholding rates on dividends, interest, or royalties that would otherwise be subject to the statutory 25% Part XIII rate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may invoke GAAR under section 245 to prevent the treaty benefit and recharacterize distributions as dividends subject to 25% Part XIII withholding. The Canada-US Treaty's Limitation on Benefits clause automatically denies treaty benefits to a shell corporation that is not a recognized resident with substantial business purpose. Application of GAAR can result in a denial of treaty reduction, a reassessment of amounts paid as royalty into deemed dividends, and a gross negligence penalty of 50% of the federal tax payable.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Because an Alberta ULC is an unlimited liability entity, any shareholder who participates in treaty-shopping using a shell ULC can be personally liable for the corporate obligations to CRA. CRA may pierce the corporate veil under common-law fraudulent conveyance and agency doctrines. Directors face civil restitution for disgorged treaty benefits, and where a financial crime has been committed, travel restrictions and criminal sanctions under the Criminal Code can be imposed.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating a real-time video-matching monetization business via Apple IAP and Paymentwall without a registered Canadian Money Service Business or FINTRAC compliance program, including failing to identify large cash-like settlement flows, failing to conduct PEP/client screening, or facilitating transactions for sanctioned counterparties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, a corporation faces administrative monetary penalties of up to CAD 250,000 per violation and criminal fines up to CAD 2,000,000 on conviction. Penalties are also available under Alberta securities and consumer protection statutes if the payment processing is used for unlawful gambling, fraud, or unlicensed money transmission.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers are personally liable if they knowingly direct, authorize, or acquiesce in AML non-compliance; the court can order them to pay restitution to the Crown and impose imprisonment up to 5 years. FINTRAC may also issue a statement of objections and the Minister may seek a court order freezing corporate and personal assets. The unlimited liability structure of the ULC means that AML penalties and disgorgement orders can be enforced directly against shareholders' personal estates.
